title: VLOOKUP Basics
description: Find a value in a table by its first column and return a matching result.
overview: VLOOKUP is the classic Excel lookup: it searches the first column of a table for a value, then returns a value from another column in the same row. This lesson focuses on exact matches and approximate band lookups so you understand when the fourth argument matters.
objectives: Write a VLOOKUP for an exact match using FALSE/0.
Understand when VLOOKUP requires sorted data and TRUE/1.
Avoid the most common VLOOKUP mistakes.

steps.heading: Choose the table
steps.body: VLOOKUP only looks in the first column of the selected range. Put your lookup values there.

steps.heading: Set the column index
steps.body: Count from the left edge of the selected range: column 2 returns the second column.

steps.heading: Pick exact or approximate
steps.body: Use 0/FALSE for exact matches. Use 1/TRUE only when the first column is sorted and you want the closest lower match.

faqs.question: Why does VLOOKUP return #N/A?
faqs.answer: Usually the lookup value is not in the first column, text/number formats differ, or you used approximate match on unsorted data.

faqs.question: Can VLOOKUP look left?
faqs.answer: No. VLOOKUP searches the first column and returns columns to the right. Use XLOOKUP or INDEX/MATCH for leftward lookups.

title: XLOOKUP Basics
description: Search any direction, return any column, and handle missing matches cleanly.
overview: XLOOKUP is the modern replacement for VLOOKUP: it can search left or right, return a column to the left, and show a custom value when no match exists. This lesson practices exact lookups and the if-not-found argument.
objectives: Write XLOOKUP with lookup array and return array.
Use the if-not-found argument for cleaner reports.
Compare XLOOKUP with VLOOKUP mentally before choosing one.

steps.heading: Separate lookup and return ranges
steps.body: Unlike VLOOKUP, the search range and result range can be different shapes as long as they align.

steps.heading: Add a default
steps.body: The fourth argument controls what appears when no match is found, replacing #N/A with text like "Not found".

steps.heading: Prefer exact match
steps.body: XLOOKUP defaults to exact matching, which prevents surprises from unsorted approximate lookups.

faqs.question: Does XLOOKUP work in older Excel?
faqs.answer: XLOOKUP requires Microsoft 365 or Excel 2021 and later. For older versions, use VLOOKUP or INDEX/MATCH.

faqs.question: Why use XLOOKUP over VLOOKUP?
faqs.answer: It is more flexible: leftward lookup, no column-index counting, exact match by default, and a built-in not-found value.

title: Text Cleanup Basics
description: Trim spaces, change case and join text values with Excel formulas.
overview: Messy text breaks lookups and reports. This lesson practices three everyday fixes: removing extra spaces with TRIM, normalizing case with UPPER, and joining values with the concatenation operator.
objectives: Remove leading and trailing spaces with TRIM.
Standardize text case with UPPER.
Combine first and last name style values in one formula.

steps.heading: Clean before you compare
steps.body: A trailing space makes "East " different from "East". TRIM first, then lookup or count.

steps.heading: Normalize case
steps.body: Use UPPER or LOWER when imported data mixes "east", "East" and "EAST".

steps.heading: Join with &
steps.body: The ampersand operator combines text and values without needing CONCAT in older Excel versions.

faqs.question: Why does my lookup fail after copying data?
faqs.answer: Extra spaces or different capitalization are common causes. Clean with TRIM and UPPER/LOWER before matching.

faqs.question: What is the difference between TRIM and CLEAN?
faqs.answer: TRIM removes extra spaces; CLEAN removes non-printable characters. Use both when data came from PDFs or web pages.

title: Date Math Basics
description: Calculate days between dates and extract the year from an Excel date serial.
overview: Excel stores dates as serial numbers, which makes date math possible with simple subtraction and functions like DAYS and YEAR. This lesson uses serial values so the practice matches how formulas actually calculate.
objectives: Use DAYS to calculate the number of days between two dates.
Extract the year from a date serial with YEAR.
Recognize why Excel dates are numbers under the hood.

steps.heading: Remember dates are numbers
steps.body: Excel stores 2026-01-01 as a serial value, so subtraction gives elapsed days.

steps.heading: Use DAYS for clarity
steps.body: DAYS(end_date, start_date) returns the difference without depending on cell subtraction direction.

steps.heading: Extract parts with YEAR/MONTH/DAY
steps.body: Use YEAR, MONTH and DAY when you need report labels or grouping by period.

faqs.question: Why is my date formula showing a number?
faqs.answer: Excel stores dates as serial numbers. Apply a date number format or wrap the result in TEXT for display.

faqs.question: Does DAYS work with text dates?
faqs.answer: It is safer to use real Excel dates or DATE() values. Text dates may not coerce consistently across locales.

title: SUMIF and COUNTIF Basics
description: Total and count only the rows that meet a condition.
overview: SUMIF and COUNTIF let a spreadsheet answer questions like 'total sales for East' or 'how many orders are over $100' without filtering the table manually. This lesson practices single-criteria totals and counts.
objectives: Write SUMIF with separate criteria and sum ranges.
Write COUNTIF with text and numeric criteria.
Know when to move from SUMIF/COUNTIF to SUMIFS/COUNTIFS.

steps.heading: Match the ranges
steps.body: In SUMIF, criteria_range and sum_range should cover the same rows even if they are different columns.

steps.heading: Quote text criteria
steps.body: Use quotes for text criteria like "East" and operators like ">100" for numbers.

steps.heading: Add criteria pairs for multiple conditions
steps.body: When one condition is not enough, use SUMIFS or COUNTIFS with range/criteria pairs.

faqs.question: Why does SUMIF return 0?
faqs.answer: Check criteria spelling, number formats, and whether the ranges start on the same row.

faqs.question: SUMIF vs SUMIFS?
faqs.answer: SUMIF handles one condition; SUMIFS handles multiple conditions and puts sum_range first.

title: Essential Shortcuts
description: Practice bold, copy and undo shortcuts on your real keyboard.

title: Filtering Basics
description: Hide rows that do not match your criteria and answer questions about a table.
overview: Filtering lets you focus on the rows that matter: show only one region, one product or one date range without deleting anything. This lesson practices the ideas behind filtering — flagging rows with IF and summarizing a filtered view with COUNTIF and SUMIF — and shows where the Filter button lives.
objectives: Understand what filtering does to a table.
Flag rows that match a condition with IF.
Count and total only the rows you care about with COUNTIF and SUMIF.

steps.heading: Pick a clean table
steps.body: Filtering works best on a range with headers in the first row and no blank rows inside the data.

steps.heading: Turn on the filter
steps.body: Select any cell in the table, then click the Filter button on the Data tab. Dropdown arrows appear in each header.

steps.heading: Choose your criteria
steps.body: Uncheck "Select All" and tick only the values you want to see, or use Text Filters / Number Filters for conditions like "greater than".

steps.heading: Summarize the visible rows
steps.body: COUNTIF and SUMIF ignore the filter and read the whole range, so use them when you want totals for a condition no matter what is visible.

faqs.question: Does filtering delete the hidden rows?
faqs.answer: No. Filtering only hides rows. Clear the filter to bring every row back — nothing is lost.

faqs.question: Why does my SUM include rows I filtered out?
faqs.answer: SUM reads the entire range regardless of which rows are hidden. Use SUBTOTAL instead if you want a total of only the visible rows.

title: SUMPRODUCT Basics
description: Multiply columns row by row and total the results in one formula.
overview: SUMPRODUCT is Excel's row-by-row calculator: it multiplies matching values across ranges and adds the products. It powers revenue totals, weighted averages and conditional sums without helper columns.
objectives: Write SUMPRODUCT for two and three ranges.
Build a weighted average with SUMPRODUCT and SUM.
Recognize when SUMPRODUCT beats a helper column.

steps.heading: Line up the ranges
steps.body: Every range must have the same shape and start on the same row, or SUMPRODUCT returns #VALUE!.

steps.heading: Let it multiply first
steps.body: SUMPRODUCT pairs the first value of each range, multiplies them, moves to the second value, and so on — then adds everything.

steps.heading: Divide for averages
steps.body: A weighted average is SUMPRODUCT(values, weights) divided by SUM(weights).

faqs.question: SUMPRODUCT vs SUM of a helper column?
faqs.answer: They give the same result, but SUMPRODUCT does it in one formula without an extra column of =A2*B2.

faqs.question: Why do I get #VALUE!?
faqs.answer: Usually the ranges have different sizes or one range contains text where the other has numbers.

title: Text Functions: LOWER, PROPER & SUBSTITUTE
description: Change letter case and replace text inside a cell with formulas.
overview: Beyond TRIM and UPPER, Excel gives you LOWER for lowercase, PROPER for title case, and SUBSTITUTE for find-and-replace inside a formula. These three cover most of the text cleanup jobs that imported data throws at you.
objectives: Convert text to lowercase with LOWER.
Title-case names with PROPER.
Replace characters or words inside text with SUBSTITUTE.

steps.heading: Pick the right case function
steps.body: UPPER shouts, LOWER whispers, PROPER capitalizes the first letter of each word.

steps.heading: Chain functions when needed
steps.body: Nest TRIM inside PROPER — =PROPER(TRIM(A1)) — to clean spaces and fix case in one formula.

steps.heading: Replace with SUBSTITUTE
steps.body: SUBSTITUTE(text, old, new) swaps every occurrence of old for new; use "" as new to delete characters.

faqs.question: PROPER vs UPPER?
faqs.answer: UPPER makes everything capital ("ADA LOVELACE"); PROPER makes "Ada Lovelace". Use PROPER for names and titles.

faqs.question: Does SUBSTITUTE change the original cell?
faqs.answer: No — it returns the changed text. Put it in another cell or use it inside a larger formula.

title: Date Functions: YEAR, MONTH, DAY & EOMONTH
description: Pull the year, month and day out of a date and find the end of any month.
overview: Excel stores dates as serial numbers, and YEAR, MONTH and DAY read the parts back out. EOMONTH jumps to the last day of any month — essential for month-end reports and billing cycles.
objectives: Extract month and day numbers with MONTH and DAY.
Use EOMONTH to find the last day of a month.
Combine DAY and EOMONTH to get a day count like 31.

steps.heading: Dates are numbers
steps.body: A date serial counts days since Excel's epoch, so YEAR, MONTH and DAY simply decode it.

steps.heading: Extract the parts
steps.body: YEAR gives 2026, MONTH gives 3, DAY gives 15 for March 15, 2026.

steps.heading: EOMONTH for month ends
steps.body: EOMONTH(date, 0) returns the last day of the same month; wrap it in DAY to read just the day number.

faqs.question: Why does EOMONTH show a number instead of a date?
faqs.answer: EOMONTH returns a serial value. Apply a date number format, or use DAY(EOMONTH(...)) if you only need the day number.

faqs.question: What does the second argument of EOMONTH do?
faqs.answer: It shifts months: 0 is the same month, 1 is next month, -1 is the previous month.

title: Percentage Calculations
description: Work out shares of a total and percent change with plain formulas.
overview: Percentages in Excel are just division: a share is part divided by total, and percent change is the difference divided by the old value. This lesson practices both, including the ×100 step and how the Percent format displays results.
objectives: Calculate a value's share of a total.
Calculate percent change between two numbers.
Understand the difference between 0.25 and 25% formatting.

steps.heading: Share of total
steps.body: Divide one value by SUM of the range: =B2/SUM($B$2:$B$4) gives a decimal like 0.3.

steps.heading: Percent change
steps.body: Use (new - old) / old. Multiply by 100 if you want 25 instead of 0.25.

steps.heading: Let the format do the work
steps.body: Apply the Percent number format to a decimal result instead of multiplying by 100 — Excel displays 0.25 as 25%.

faqs.question: Why does my percent show 3000% instead of 30%?
faqs.answer: You multiplied by 100 AND applied Percent format, which multiplies by 100 again. Pick one or the other.

faqs.question: How do I keep the denominator fixed when copying?
faqs.answer: Use absolute references like $B$2:$B$4 so the total range does not shift.

title: Find and Substitute
description: Replace text across a sheet with the Find & Replace dialog and SUBSTITUTE.
overview: Two ways to fix repeated text problems: the Find and Replace dialog (Ctrl+H) changes cells directly, while SUBSTITUTE does it inside a formula so the original data stays intact. This lesson practices SUBSTITUTE and when to reach for each tool.
objectives: Open Find and Replace with Ctrl+H.
Use SUBSTITUTE to replace text inside a formula.
Choose between the dialog and the formula for a cleanup job.

steps.heading: For quick fixes, use the dialog
steps.body: Ctrl+H opens Find and Replace. Type the text to find, the replacement, and click Replace All.

steps.heading: For formulas, use SUBSTITUTE
steps.body: =SUBSTITUTE(A1,"-","/") returns the changed text without touching the original cell.

steps.heading: Replace every occurrence
steps.body: SUBSTITUTE and Replace All both swap every match — there is no "first only" option in SUBSTITUTE.

faqs.question: Find & Replace vs SUBSTITUTE?
faqs.answer: Find & Replace edits the cells themselves. SUBSTITUTE returns new text inside a formula, which is safer when the original data must stay unchanged.

faqs.question: Can I replace across an entire workbook?
faqs.answer: Yes — in the Find and Replace dialog choose "Workbook" in the Within dropdown.

title: Named Ranges Basics
description: Give cells and ranges meaningful names and use them in formulas.
overview: A named range turns =SUM(B2:B4) into =SUM(Sales) — formulas that read like sentences and survive inserted rows. This lesson covers what makes a valid name, how names behave in formulas, and the difference between workbook and worksheet scope.
objectives: Know the rules for a valid defined name.
Use a named range anywhere a cell reference works.
Understand workbook vs worksheet scope.

steps.heading: Select and name
steps.body: Select the cell or range, then type the name into the Name Box (left of the formula bar) and press Enter.

steps.heading: Follow the naming rules
steps.body: Start with a letter or underscore, use letters, numbers and dots — no spaces, and never a cell reference like A1.

steps.heading: Use it like a reference
steps.body: A name works anywhere a range works: =Sales*1.1, =SUM(Sales), or inside VLOOKUP.

faqs.question: What happens to a name when I insert rows?
faqs.answer: The name keeps pointing at the same logical range — Excel adjusts the reference automatically, which is a big advantage over hard-coded ranges in formulas.

faqs.question: Why is my name not working in a formula?
faqs.answer: Check the spelling, make sure it does not look like a cell reference, and confirm the scope includes the sheet you are on.

title: Sorting and Filtering
description: Order a table and hide what you do not need with Sort and Filter.
overview: Sorting rearranges rows so the biggest or newest values surface first; filtering hides the rest. Together they turn a raw table into a report you can read at a glance — and SMALL/LARGE give you the sorted answers without moving anything.
objectives: Sort a column ascending or descending.
Predict where values land after a sort.
Use SMALL and LARGE to read sorted positions from formulas.

steps.heading: Sort smallest to largest
steps.body: Select the column, then Data > Sort Smallest to Largest (or the Z-A / A-Z equivalents for text).

steps.heading: Watch where extremes land
steps.body: After ascending sort the smallest value sits on top and the largest on the bottom; descending flips it.

steps.heading: Filter to focus
steps.body: Filter dropdowns let you tick only the values you want; Clear Filter brings everything back.

steps.heading: Formulas see the unsorted truth
steps.body: SMALL(range, 2) returns the second smallest value no matter how the rows are arranged.

faqs.question: Does sorting change my formulas?
faqs.answer: No — formulas reference cells by position, so results stay the same; only the visual order changes.

faqs.question: Sort vs Filter?
faqs.answer: Sort reorders rows; Filter hides rows you do not want to see. You can use both on the same table.
